solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Feel lot going wrong, including spar? Gremlin possibly (12, two words)

indicators.note: something going wrong falls out of its proper order, so the letters are rearranged
including means taking another piece inside, so one set of letters wraps around the other

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
a sprit is a spar that extends a sail diagonally

explanation.surface: Someone senses a lot going wrong around a ship's spar and blames a gremlin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spar' here is a sail's sprit, not a boxing bout; it sits inside the shuffled letters, which split either side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An esprit follet is a mischievous goblin or sprite in French folklore, of which a gremlin is a modern example.

clue.text: The old plunge in river emerging from spring

indicators.note: something emerging from a place has left it, so that letter comes out of the larger word

blocks.note: R is the usual abbreviation for river
a spring is the source of a stream

explanation.surface: An old dip into a river where it rises from a spring.
explanation.walkthrough: Take R out of SOURCE to leave SOUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Souce is an obsolete spelling of souse, to plunge or dip into liquid, hence 'the old' marking an archaic form.

clue.text: Mooch historically as Prince, endless reign containing nothing

indicators.note: endless means without its final letter, so the last letter is dropped
containing means holding something inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for prince
to reign is to rule
O is the figure for nothing

explanation.surface: A prince loafs about, his reign cut short and amounting to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: RULE loses its last letter to give RUL, which holds O: ROUL, after P.
explanation.definitionFit: Proul is an old spelling of prowl, to roam about idly, which is what mooching means.

clue.text: Hammered peat floor, whereon rafter rests (9, two words)

indicators.note: something hammered is beaten out of shape, so its letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A beaten earth floor in a cottage, with the rafters above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A roof plate is the horizontal timber along the top of a wall that the feet of the rafters sit on.

clue.text: Rag suggesting leaders from The Times to audience

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters, so only the initial of each word is kept
something put to an audience is heard rather than seen, so what is said matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: the two initials are a pair of Ts, spoken as tees

explanation.surface: A newspaper's banter is put to its readers.
explanation.walkthrough: The leaders of The Times are T and T, two tees, and said aloud that is TEASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To rag someone is to mock or make fun of them, which is to tease them.

clue.text: Harmful worms almost cram a valley

definitions.note: plural: filaria names the genus of these parasitic worms

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is left off

blocks.note: to cram is to fill
taken as written
a ria is a drowned river valley

explanation.surface: Parasitic worms nearly fill a whole valley.
explanation.walkthrough: A ria is a river valley drowned by the sea, a common crossword word for valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Filaria are threadlike parasitic nematode worms that cause diseases such as elephantiasis, so harmful is apt.

clue.text: Facing king's left in card game

indicators.note: left means gone away, so the named word departs from the longer one

blocks.note: a house facing south is looking south
taken as written

explanation.surface: At cards, the player opposite the king sits to his left.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as 'looking with king's departed': remove KING from LOOKING. The 's is 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Loo, short for lanterloo, is an old gambling card game played for a pool of stakes.

clue.text: Femme fatale that is turning up in support of good-for-nothing

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
in a down answer, supporting means sitting underneath, so this piece comes after the other

blocks.note: lorel is an old word for a worthless person, a losel
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A seductress turns up to back some useless man.
explanation.walkthrough: IE reversed gives EI, placed below LOREL in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is the siren of Rhine legend who lured boatmen to their deaths, the archetypal femme fatale.

clue.text: Cheering such as welcomes M. Antony's speech

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in a guest, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: e.g. means 'for example', such as
Marcus Antonius, a Roman, would have spoken Latin

explanation.surface: The crowd cheers Mark Antony's famous funeral oration.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' speech, but 'speech' here means the language a Roman spoke.
explanation.definitionFit: Elating means making someone joyful or in high spirits, as cheering does.

clue.text: Spongy place round moor, half submerged

indicators.note: with half of the word sunk out of sight, only the other half is left to use
round means going around the outside, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to pose a thing is to place it, set it down
the second half of the word moor

explanation.surface: A boggy patch around moorland lies half under water.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of moor sinks out of sight; only its second half is used, wrapped inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Porose is a variant of porous, full of pores, which is what a spongy material is.

clue.text: Pin-up maybe excited ogler with strip (10, two words)

indicators.note: something excited is stirred up and agitated, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: part of the anagram fodder, taken as written
the rest of the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A leering man gets worked up over a striptease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excited' seems to describe the ogler, and 'strip' to be a striptease, but both words are just letters to jumble together.
explanation.definitionFit: A poster girl is an attractive woman pictured on a poster, and a pin-up is one example.

clue.text: Cash needed to get a weaver's machine turning

indicators.note: turning round means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
a loom is the machine a weaver uses

explanation.surface: A weaver needs money to keep the loom going.
explanation.definitionFit: Moola is slang for money, so it means cash.

clue.text: A final dance with date one embraced? What a sad time! (10, three words)

indicators.note: something embraced is held in someone's arms, so these letters sit inside the dance word

blocks.note: taken as written
final means last
a hey (or hay) is an old country dance in which dancers weave in and out
D is the abbreviation for date
a means one, as in 'a dozen'

explanation.surface: A last dance with your date, holding them close: how sad that the evening ends.
explanation.walkthrough: A hey is an old country dance, also spelt hay, and 'one' is the article a.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Alas the day!' is an archaic exclamation of grief or regret, lamenting an unhappy occasion.

clue.text: Petticoat causing guessing game in the course of dance

indicators.note: something happening in the course of an event takes place within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance
mora is a game in which players guess how many fingers are held up

explanation.surface: A woman's petticoat prompts speculation during a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: Mora is an ancient Italian game of guessing the number of fingers shown.
explanation.definitionFit: A balmoral was a woollen petticoat worn under a looped-up skirt, named after the royal Scottish castle.

clue.text: Where sucker-punch has landed, tender? Copper shown for nothing

indicators.note: one thing shown for another stands in its place, so a letter is swapped out

blocks.note: tender means soft
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
O is the figure for nothing

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether the spot hit by an unfair blow is sore; a policeman turns up to no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: CU replaces O in SOFT. The definition is cryptic: a sucker-punch is a blow from behind, so it lands on the back of the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: Scuft is a dialect word for the nape or scruff of the neck, the spot a blow from behind would strike.

clue.text: Eject clique round priest

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one piece goes about the other

blocks.note: a set is a clique, a social group
P is the abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: A clique gathers around a priest to throw him out.
explanation.definitionFit: Spet is a Scots and obsolete form of spit, to eject from the mouth.

clue.text: In translation a poem about queen in part of Poland

indicators.note: a translation renders the words in a new form, so the letters are rearranged
about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the other piece

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
a rani is an Indian queen

explanation.surface: A poem about a queen, translated, is set in a part of Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters of A POEM split either side of RANI.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomerania is a historic region on the Baltic coast, most of which now lies in northern Poland.

clue.text: Cable-car system, maybe help when working in region short of rain

indicators.note: working means being worked on and reshaped, so the letters are rearranged
short of means lacking, so those letters are taken away from the word
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
terrain is a region of land
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A cable car might help people get about a region with little rain.
explanation.walkthrough: TERRAIN without RAIN leaves TER, which holds the rearranged HELP.
explanation.definitionFit: A telpher is a system of overhead cables carrying cars or loads, so a cable-car system is one example.

clue.text: I'll be nabbed by copper back in Irish force?

indicators.note: someone nabbed is caught and held, so this letter is placed inside the other word
back means going in the reverse direction, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: slop is back slang for a policeman
I will be: the letter I

explanation.surface: An Irishman wonders if he will be arrested by a policeman back home.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes inside SLOP, then the whole is reversed. Slop comes from back slang, police read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Polis is the Irish and Scots pronunciation and spelling of police, the force that keeps order.

clue.text: Opioid substance even after measure of fish that's given a lift

indicators.note: in a down answer, lifting means raising from the bottom up, so the letters read upwards
after means coming later, so this piece follows the other

blocks.note: a cran is a measure of fresh herrings, about 750 fish
e'en is the poetic contraction of even

explanation.surface: A fisherman's catch gets a boost from some drug.
explanation.walkthrough: CRAN read upwards gives NARC, followed by EEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Narceen (narceine) is a bitter alkaloid found in opium, so it is an opioid substance.

clue.text: Hollywood wannabes leaving out pound for spiritual guide

indicators.note: leaving out means omitting, so that letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: starlets are young actresses hoping for stardom
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: Aspiring actors dodge paying for a guru.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop L from STARLETS.
explanation.definitionFit: A starets is an elder of the Russian Orthodox Church revered as a spiritual teacher and adviser.

clue.text: Baron's complaint following delivery of goods in trust

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for baron
an ailment is an illness, a complaint

explanation.surface: A nobleman's illness follows a shipment.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's simply joins baron to his complaint: B then AILMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, bailment is handing goods to another person to hold for a purpose, on trust that they will be returned.

clue.text: Constant gold buried in cryptic plan, with which 'the hills are alive'?

indicators.note: cryptic means obscure and coded, so the letters are scrambled
something buried in another thing lies inside it, so these letters go within

blocks.note: h is Planck's constant in physics
or is gold in heraldry
the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A treasure hidden in a secret scheme is linked to the line from The Sound of Music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The hills are alive with the sound of music' is the opening song of The Sound of Music, set in the Alps; the definition is playful, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The alphorn is a long wooden horn blown by Alpine herdsmen, whose sound fills the mountains.

clue.text: Tattoo went round palm, left

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the first word encloses the others

blocks.note: ran means went, as a bus runs
atap is the nipa palm, whose leaves are used for thatch
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone got a tattoo inked around their hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tattoo' and 'palm' suggest body art, but the tattoo is a drumbeat and the palm a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A rataplan is the rattling beat of a drum, and a tattoo is a drum signal recalling soldiers to quarters.

clue.text: Wicket restricting runs making one fret

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: a wicket is a small gate
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricket pitch that limits scoring frustrates the batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket wicket is a red herring: a wicket is also a small gate or door.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that grates irritates, so to grate is to annoy, making a person fret.

clue.text: Flint (say) with opening for start of combustion in explosive stuff

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
an opening made for something lets it in, so a letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: Captain Flint is the pirate in Treasure Island; 'say' marks him as an example
the first letter of combustion

explanation.surface: A flint's spark starts a fire in some explosive material.
explanation.walkthrough: Flint looks like the fire-striking stone, but it is Long John Silver's old captain. C goes inside PIRATE after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A picrate is a salt of picric acid, and many picrates are used as explosives.

clue.text: Pub with attractive quality? It doesn't mean much

blocks.note: an inn is a pub
it is sex appeal, as in the 'It girl'

explanation.surface: A charming pub isn't really important.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole final sentence, with 'It' innocently capitalised as the start of a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Innit, from 'isn't it', is a slang tag tacked onto sentences with little real meaning.

clue.text: One from the north in a sort of cravat?

blocks.note: a means one
a Scot comes from the north of Britain

explanation.surface: A Scotsman dressed in a broad neckscarf.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits a light touch: the whole clue is a picture of a Scot in an ascot, while A plus SCOT build the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad neck scarf worn looped under the chin, a kind of cravat named after the racecourse.

clue.text: Part of intercession that features in the Divine Office

definitions.text: that features in the Divine Office

indicators.note: part of means a piece of the following word, so the letters lie within it

blocks.note: letters three to seven of this word

explanation.surface: Prayer for others is one element of the Church's daily liturgy.
explanation.definitionFit: Terce is the canonical hour of prayer said at the third hour, about 9am, one of the services of the Divine Office.

clue.text: Ship's company prison officers released from ship's hold

indicators.note: something released from a grip is let go, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: screws is slang for prison warders
SS, steamship, is the ship; its two letters hold the word between them

explanation.surface: Sailors are let go after warders have taken over the hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The ship's 'hold' is not its cargo space: SS brackets the middle letters, and releasing them frees what lies between.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's company is everyone who works aboard, i.e. its crew.

clue.text: Relaxed, taking some tea sedately

indicators.note: taking some of the words means using just a portion of them, so the letters lie inside

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone unwinds by drinking tea slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: Eased means relaxed, loosened, with tension taken away.

clue.text: Rook and eider nod off (not I) in waterside thicket

indicators.note: not I means without that letter, so it is removed
off means wrong or out of kilter, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: R is the chess abbreviation for rook
the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A rook and an eider duck doze off by the reeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I from EIDER NOD, then rearrange the rest after R.
explanation.definitionFit: A reedrond is a thicket of reeds growing by water, a dialect word recorded in Chambers.

clue.text: Partner to carry climbing ivy bush?

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means going upwards, so the letters read in reverse

blocks.note: a tod is a thick bush, especially of ivy

explanation.surface: Ivy climbs a shrub that serves as a support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dot and carry' is the old schoolroom phrase for adding up, so dot is carry's partner.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'dot and carry', dot partners carry as its regular companion word in the phrase.

clue.text: Reveal one alone denied sing (5, two words)

indicators.note: denied means refused, so the word is withheld from the longer one

blocks.note: a singleton is a single person or thing on its own
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A soloist refused the chance to sing tells all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing' looks like a synonym for reveal, as an informer sings, but it is the part to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: To let on is an idiom for disclosing a secret, i.e. to reveal it.

clue.text: I do shiver in very cold folly

indicators.note: to shiver is to shatter into pieces, so the letters are broken up and reassembled
in places the rearranged letters inside the other word

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
icy means very cold

explanation.surface: Someone admits to shivering in freezing weather out of foolishness.
explanation.walkthrough: Shiver looks like what one does in the cold, but it means smash to pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiocy is extreme foolishness, a synonym for folly.

clue.text: Exemplified opponent creating division, placed in office?

indicators.note: dividing a word splits it in two, so the other piece goes into the gap

blocks.note: to instate is to put someone into an office
an anti is someone opposed to something

explanation.surface: An opponent of the leader splits the party once installed in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed in office' looks like part of the definition with a question mark, but it is the word being divided.
explanation.definitionFit: To instantiate is to represent by a concrete instance, so instantiated means given as an example.
